summary: In Greek mythology, Amphimachus (Ancient Greek Ἀμφίμαχος) son of Nomion is co-captain, with his brother Nastes, of the Carian contingent that holds Miletus, Phthires, the Maeander, and Mycale for Troy. Homer's Catalogue describes one of the brothers coming to war decked in gold "like a girl"; commentators disagree which brother Achilles then slays and strips.
attribution: Adapted from Wikipedia, "Amphimachus of Caria" · CC BY-SA 4.0
etymology: Greek Ἀμφίμαχος from ἀμφί and μάχη; Homer's twin captains are "the glorious children of Nomion."

sections.heading: Carian captains
paragraphs: Iliad 2.867–875 names Amphimachus and Nastes, sons of Nomion, leaders of the Carians "uncouth of speech" who held Miletus and leafy Phthires, the streams of Maeander, and Mycale's steep crests. One brother arrives all decked with gold; the gold does not save him — Achilles slays him in the river and bears the gold away.

Ancient and modern readers divide on whether Amphimachus or Nastes is the gold-wearing victim. The atlas keeps Amphimachus as Nomion's named co-captain of Miletus without forcing the Catalogue's ambiguous "he" onto one brother alone.

sections.heading: Homonym care
paragraphs: The atlas id amphimachus-nomionid is the Carian son of Nomion alone. Distinct from amphimachus-epeian (Cteatus' Elean leader slain by Hector) and from other Amphimachus namesakes.
